To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) maraviroc (MVC) decreased the plasma concentrations of bacterial products in HIV-infected patients, and 2) this decrease was not linked to an increased immune activation.

maraviroc (MVC)-treated HIV-infected individuals had lower plasma levels of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), but similar plasma levels of soluble CD14 and soluble toll-like receptor 2 compared with untreated controls.

maraviroc treatment did not increase the levels of immune activation biomarkers and that the decrease in bacterial products observed with maraviroc was not associated with a decrease in the levels of immune markers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of maraviroc on the levels of bacterial products in HIV-infected patients and whether these effects are linked to immune activation.
the effects of the CCR5 inhibitor maraviroc on the immune system in the context of HIV infection.
the effect of maraviroc on circulating bacterial products and immune activation in HIV-1-infected patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of maraviroc in HIV-infected patients is not associated with a significant increase in immune activation.
the use of maraviroc is not associated with increased immune activation in patients with HIV infection, which is in line with the results of the MERIT study.
there is no evidence that maraviroc is associated with an increase in immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the decrease in circulating bacterial components in maraviroc (MVC) treated patients did not correlate with an increase in immune activity.
the decrease in circulating bacterial components after maraviroc treatment is not linked to a decrease in the immune activation in the HIV-infected individuals.
maraviroc (MVC)-induced decrease in circulating bacterial product (CP) levels is not linked to a decrease in immune activation in MVC-treated HIV-infected individuals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
maraviroc, when used in combination with antiretroviral therapy, does not increase immune activation, as measured by plasma levels of sCD14, IL-6, and TNF-α.
maraviroc, when used as a part of a suppressive antiretroviral regimen, is associated with a decrease in circulating bacterial cell wall products.
HIV infection is associated with an increase in bacterial translocation and that maraviroc (MVC) can decrease bacterial translocation in a subset of HIV-infected individuals (1).
